{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=What+are+the+common+failure+modes+and+risks+associated+with+autonomous+systems+identifying+knowledge+gaps+without+human+supervision%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"title\": [\"When Agentic AI Breaks Software Quality Assurance: Failure Modes, Reliability Risks, and Governance Strategies for Autonomous Testing Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing software quality assurance from a predominantly human-directed activity into an increasingly autonomous process in which AI systems can generate tests, execute programs, interpret failures, modify test suites, and iteratively refine their actions. While these capabilities promise substantial improvements in testing speed, coverage, and engineering productivity, they also introduce a distinct class of quality risks. An autonomous testing agent can produce a technically executable test that encodes an incorrect assumption, misinterpret a failure, optimize for coverage rather than meaningful defect detection, or repeatedly reinforce an erroneous testing strategy. This article examines these risks through an integrative review of research on large language models (LLMs), automated software testing, AI-assisted software engineering, and AI governance. The analysis identifies six interconnected failure modes: erroneous test generation, defective test oracles, autonomous error propagation, coverage-driven quality illusion, contextual and repository misunderstanding, and governance and accountability failure. The article argues that the central challenge is not simply whether AI can generate valid tests, but whether autonomous testing systems can maintain trustworthy quality judgments under uncertainty. Drawing on empirical evidence from recent studies of ChatGPT, LLM-based test generation, TestGen-LLM, and software-engineering agents, the article proposes a risk-based governance model built around bounded autonomy, independent verification, traceability, human checkpoints, continuous monitoring, and explicit escalation mechanisms. The findings suggest that enterprise adoption should treat agentic testing as a controlled socio-technical system rather than a replacement for software quality expertise.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/nini8845\", \"title\": [\"Filling Knowledge Gaps in Human-Robot Interaction Using Rewritten Knowledge of Common Verbs: Extended Abstract\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>In this paper, we present an approach to representing a core part of the knowledge consists of semantic information of common verbs from semantic dictionaries. We provide a meta-language as the representation framework for the rewritten knowledge of common verbs and their corresponding user tasks. The meta-language is interpreted based on transition systems, which can be realized on various formalizations such as situation calculus, action languages, and answer set planning. We realize the approach based on answer set planning. Moreover, we provide empirical evidence showing that HRI may significantly benefit from the rewritten knowledge and remarkable performance improvement compared to previous work.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/nini8845\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2015, 5, 4]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/979-8-8688-2839-3_11\", \"title\": [\"Common Design Risks and Failure Modes in Serverless Distributed Systems\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/979-8-8688-2839-3_11\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7248799\", \"title\": [\"A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Autonomous Agentic Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Autonomous agentic systems transform language-model outputs into sequences of state-changing actions. This shift changes the failure problem: a locally plausible response can become a globally incorrect plan, a corrupted memory, an unauthorized tool call, an irreversible side effect, or a false declaration of success. Existing research has documented important fragments of this landscapelong-horizon degradation, tool-use errors, multi-agent coordination breakdowns, prompt injection, memory poisoning, weak self-verification, and emergent misalignment-but operational teams still lack a compact systems taxonomy that connects these findings to observable failure surfaces and engineering controls. \\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n We propose AFT-32, an evidence-grounded taxonomy containing 32 failure modes across eight families: intent and specification; perception and state estimation; reasoning and planning; tool and action execution; memory and context; coordination and delegation; verification and termination; and security, alignment, and authority. We further introduce crosscutting modifiers for origin, temporal behavior, detectability, scope, recoverability, and consequence; a closed-loop model of agent failure; and a deployment-oriented testing and control framework. The central conclusion is that reliable agency cannot be obtained by model capability alone. It requires explicit authority boundaries, trustworthy state, fault-aware tool integration, independent verification, bounded loops, provenance-preserving memory, and system-level observability. AFT-32 is intended as a shared vocabulary for researchers, red teams, platform engineers, and governance teams designing evaluations and safety cases for increasingly autonomous systems.\\n</div></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7248799\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "f8ba6163d4d7a6a0043eb7675b07204cc59c7341199e1072f8907bf99a9f2ab8", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_inquiry", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7433399", "doi:10.65109/nini8845", "doi:10.1007/979-8-8688-2839-3_11", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7248799"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7433399", "https://doi.org/10.65109/nini8845", "https://doi.org/10.1007/979-8-8688-2839-3_11", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7248799"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
